summary: Sherwood Callaway and Satwik Singh from 11x present 'Building Alice's Brain,' describing how they built an AI sales rep that learns like a human. 11x builds digital workers for go-to-market teams; their products include Alice (AI SDR) and Julian (voice agent). Alice sends roughly 50,000 emails per day across 300+ organizations, compared to a human SDR's 20-50. The talk clarifies terminology: the 'seller' is 11x's customer, and the 'lead' is the person being sold to. Previously, sellers used a manual 'library' to push context to Alice by hand-entering details about every product, pain point, and value prop. This was tedious, caused onboarding friction, and produced sub-optimal emails due to too few or too many offers in context. The solution is a knowledge base: a centralized repository where sellers upload source materials and Alice retrieves relevant context at message generation time. The pipeline has five steps: parsing, chunking, storage, retrieval, and visualization. For parsing, 11x chose vendor-based solutions over building in-house, selecting LlamaParse for documents/images (best file-type support and responsive support), Firecrawl for websites (familiarity and Tavily's crawl endpoint was still in development), and Cloudglue for audio/video (supports both audio and video and extracts visual information beyond just transcripts). All resources are converted to markdown. For chunking, they use a waterfall strategy: split on markdown headers, then sentences, then tokens, preserving semantic structure while controlling chunk size for embedding. For storage, they chose Pinecone as their vector database because it was well-known, cloud-hosted, easy to start, bundled embedding models, and had great customer support. For retrieval, they evolved from traditional RAG to a deep research agent built with Leta, which plans multi-step context retrieval and summarizes results in Q&A format. For visualization, they built an interactive 3D projection of Pinecone vectors that lets users click nodes to inspect chunks, reassuring customers that Alice knows their business. Key lessons: RAG is complex with many micro-decisions, get to production before benchmarking, and lean on vendors to learn and negotiate. Future plans include tracking hallucinations, evaluating parsing accuracy/completeness, experimenting with hybrid RAG (graph + vector), and reducing pipeline costs.

sections.title: Introduction and 11x Overview
sections.summary: Sherwood introduces himself and Satwik as tech leads at 11x, which builds digital workers for go-to-market teams. They have Alice (AI SDR) and Julian (voice agent), with more workers coming.

sections.title: SDR Role and Alice's Scale
sections.summary: Defines an SDR as an entry-level sales role responsible for sourcing leads, engaging across channels, and booking meetings. Key metrics are positive replies and meetings booked. Alice sends ~50,000 emails/day for 300+ organizations, versus a human SDR's 20-50.

sections.title: Terminology, Requirements, and the Old Library
sections.summary: Defines 'seller' (11x's customer) and 'lead' (person being sold to). Alice must know both the seller and the lead. Describes the old manual 'library' where users entered every product, service, pain point, and value prop by hand, and how offers were selected during campaign creation.

sections.title: Library Problems and Knowledge Base Idea
sections.summary: The old library was tedious, caused onboarding friction, and produced sub-optimal emails (too few or too many offers in context). The new idea: Alice proactively pulls context about the seller into her system and uses what's most relevant when writing emails.

sections.title: Knowledge Base Overview and Architecture
sections.summary: The knowledge base is a centralized repository for seller info. Architecture: upload to S3, backend creates DB records, async vendor parsing via webhooks, store in DB and upsert to Pinecone with embeddings, agent queries Pinecone at generation time.

sections.title: Pipeline and Parsing Deep Dive
sections.summary: Pipeline has five steps: parsing, chunking, storage, retrieval, visualization. Parsing converts non-text resources to markdown. 11x chose vendor-based parsing over in-house. Requirements: resource-type support, markdown output, webhooks. Did not initially consider accuracy, comprehensiveness, or cost. Selected LlamaParse for documents and images.

sections.title: Parsing Vendors: LlamaParse, Firecrawl, Cloudglue
sections.summary: LlamaParse was chosen for documents/images due to best file-type support and great support responsiveness. Firecrawl was chosen for websites over Tavily because of familiarity and Tavily's crawl endpoint still being in development. Cloudglue was chosen for audio/video because it supports both formats and extracts visual information beyond just audio transcripts. All produce markdown output.

sections.title: Chunking Strategy
sections.summary: Chunking breaks markdown blobs into semantic entities for embedding while preserving markdown structure. Strategies include splitting on tokens, sentences, markdown headers, or LLM-based splitting. 11x uses a waterfall approach: split on markdown headers, then sentences, then tokens, to control chunk token count while preserving structure. This works across all resource types and prevents super long chunks that dilute meaning.

sections.title: Storage: Pinecone Selection
sections.summary: Storage uses a vector database for similarity search, though RAG can also use graph databases, document databases, relational databases, key-value stores, or object storage. Pinecone was chosen as a well-known, cloud-hosted, easy-to-start solution with bundled embedding models and excellent customer support. The team was new to the space and chose the market leader.

sections.title: Retrieval: Evolution to Deep Research RAG
sections.summary: RAG techniques evolved from traditional RAG (pull context and enrich system prompt) to agentic RAG (tools attached to agent flows) to deep research RAG (agents plan and execute multi-step retrieval). 11x built a deep research agent using Leta, a cloud agent provider. The agent receives lead info, creates a plan with retrieval steps, calls tools, summarizes results, and generates Q&A answers.

sections.title: Visualization: Peeking into Alice's Brain
sections.summary: Visualization addresses customer trust: customers want assurance Alice knows their products and won't fabricate case studies or pain points. 11x built an interactive 3D visualization projecting Pinecone vectors down to three dimensions, where users click nodes to view associated chunks. The UI includes a modal for uploading resources, a 'learn' button, and a Q&A interface for interrogating Alice's knowledge. During campaign creation, retrieved chunks appear as expandable Q&A content showing exactly what informed the messaging.

sections.title: Conclusion, Lessons Learned, and Future Plans
sections.summary: Three key lessons: RAG is complex with many micro-decisions and vendor evaluations; get to production before benchmarking then iterate; lean on vendors and make them earn your business. Future plans: track and address email hallucinations, evaluate parsing vendors on accuracy and completeness, experiment with hybrid RAG (graph database alongside vector database), and reduce pipeline costs. 11x is hiring.
